newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO oversees sweeping pact to free infotech trade.
newsitem.headline: WTO oversees sweeping pact to free infotech trade.

text.p: A ground-breaking agreement to free global commerce in information technology and hard-won compromises among world trade ministers on Thursday capped an agenda to liberalise trade into the 21st century.

"We got everything," a beaming World Trade Organisation (WTO) Director General Renato Ruggiero told Reuters as he began a final late-night meeting with heads of delegations on the fourth day of the body's inaugural Ministerial Conference.

At the meeting, senior officials from the 128 WTO states agreed to approve a text of a Ministerial Declaration which included phrasing on labour standards which had been fiercely resisted to the last moment by some developing countries.

The declaration, a blueprint for moving the world to freer trade in the 21st century under the umbrella of the Geneva-based WTO, will be formally approved by a plenary session of the conference on Friday.
Getting the labour issue into the document had been a key aim of the United States. But U.S. officials declined to claim victory. "We are satisfied, that's all," one said.

The Information Technology Agreement (ITA), reached after four days of intense, round-the-clock talks, marked the most far-reaching accord on free trade in a single sector and should slash prices not only on high-technology but on goods from cars to cameras to washing machines.

The agreement to scrap tariffs on an estimated $600 billion in trade of information technology by the year 2000 emerged as the crowning achievement of the December 9-13 meeting, rewarding months of hard U.S. campaigning.
Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said the benefits to world trade would far exceed the financial savings from tariff reductions.
"The extent of tariff savings, which I guess would be quite hefty, doesn't begin to measure the ultimate economic benefits of agreements of this sort," she said.

"This is the biggest trade step forward...that has happened since the end of the Uruguay Round," EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said, referring to the negotiations from 1986 to 1993 that produced a wide-ranging world trade pact.
"It will be good for the IT industry, and will act as a catalyst for industrial growth," he said. "As such it will be good for the whole world economy."

The breakthrough came when Brittan won endorsement from the 15-member European Union Council for a compromise deal seen as boosting U.S. corporate profits and benefiting Asia's tiger economies. Europe stood to lose most since it has among the highest tariff levels in the world.

European officials said final agreement still depended on enough countries -- those representing about 90 percent of world trade in the sector -- joining the pact by March 15, 1997. They saw 85 percent signing the agreement by Friday.

Compromise between the United States and Europe produced a deal covering the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment -- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials.

The deal was expected to boost U.S. and European company profits and the WTO meeting drew criticism from Third World development groups, which said "corporate greed" won out and the world's poor were left to suffer.
Developing nations felt left out by the big powers. Venezuela made a strong statement protesting the "closed nature" of the negotiations, one envoy said.

Differences over discussion in the WTO of competition and investment policies and how national authorities award contracts -- government procurement -- were resolved on Wednesday, although labour and agriculture went down to the wire.

The declaration's wording will recognise the commitment of WTO countries to core labour standards but say they reject use of trade measures for protectionist purposes and would not work to deprive low-wage states of their competitive advantages.

"We are happy with what has come out," said Pakistan's Commerce Minister Muhammad Zubair Khan, and the Geneva ambassador of another key hold-out Egypt told reporters: "I think our concerns are reflected."
Other officials said the final moves to an agreement came when the core group of holdouts -- India, Pakistan and Egypt -- -- found they had little support left.

But Pakistan said it excpected a clarifying reference on labour in the statement to be issued by the conference chairman, Yeo Cheow Tong, after the declaration is formally approved by a plenary session on Friday.

Diplomats said this would say that there would be no follow-up work on the issue. "But that is not binding and the Americans have already said no-one can ever be stopped from raising anything in the WTO," said a developing country envoy.
